prompt: A student measures the diameter of a uniform wire five times using a micrometer that has an uncorrected positive zero error of +0.03 mm. The student calculates the mean of the five raw readings. What is the effect of calculating the mean on the errors in the measurement?
options: It eliminates the zero error and reduces the effect of random variations.
It reduces the effect of random variations but leaves the zero error unaffected.
It eliminates both the systematic zero error and all random errors.
It has no effect on either random variations or the systematic zero error.

answer.explanation: Calculating the mean allows random positive and negative variations to cancel partially, reducing random error. However, every reading contains the same +0.03 mm offset, so the mean retains the full zero error.

distractor_explanations: Averaging cannot remove a systematic error because the offset is identical in every measurement.
Correct. Averaging reduces the effect of random scatter, but the systematic zero error persists in the mean.
Neither error is completely eliminated, and systematic error is not reduced at all by averaging.
Averaging does reduce the effect of random fluctuations.
hints: Ask: does every single reading contain the +0.03 mm offset?
What happens to random positive and negative variations when summed and divided?
solution: Calculating the mean reduces the effect of random variations, but leaves the systematic zero error in the mean.
teacher_walkthrough: Each measurement contains: True value + Systematic offset + Random variation.
When averaged: the random variations tend to cancel out, reducing their net effect.
The systematic offset (+0.03 mm) is identical in all terms, so it remains in the average.

provenance.independence_statement: Authored to test the core distinction between remedies for random and systematic errors.
